clue.text: Old coat of rags concealing ample bust for models

indicators.note: to conceal is to hide inside, so one piece wraps around the other

parts.note: ex- means former or old

indicators.note: a coat is the outside layer, so only the outermost letters of the word are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word

indicators.note: something bust is broken, so its letters are smashed and put back together differently

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A tatty old coat stretched over a large bust, worn by fashion models.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ample bust' reads as a body part, but 'bust' is the signal to break up the word; 'Old' and the coat letters join to make the outer layer.
explanation.definitionFit: Exemplars are examples worth copying, the sense of models as patterns to imitate.

clue.text: Fetching dresses make an impression

indicators.note: to dress something is to clothe it, so the outer word wraps around the answer inside it

parts.note: the letters sit inside this word

explanation.surface: An attractive outfit catches the eye and makes a strong impression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fetching dresses' looks like attractive clothes, but 'dresses' is a verb: fETCHing wears the answer inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To etch is to cut lines into a hard surface, literally leaving a mark or indentation.

clue.text: As it happens, revolutionary is wrong

indicators.note: a revolution turns something right round, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a broadcast shown as it happens is live

explanation.surface: A remark that, as things turn out, being a revolutionary is wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As it happens' feels like a throwaway phrase, but it defines live, as in a live broadcast.
explanation.definitionFit: Evil as a noun means wickedness or wrongdoing, matching wrong used as a noun for misdeed.

clue.text: Mug knocked over with hot drink left for Easter

indicators.note: something knocked over ends up upside down, so the word is turned back to front

parts.note: a mug is a gullible fool, as is a sap
cha is a British slang word for tea
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A mug of hot chocolate knocked over and left behind at Easter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mug' looks like a cup to go with the drink, but it means a dupe.
explanation.definitionFit: Paschal is the adjective relating to Easter or Passover, from the Latin for the festival.

clue.text: Model answer about writer

indicators.note: about can mean turned round, so the joined pieces are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: to model for an artist is to pose
A is the abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: A sample answer discussing an author, as in an exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model answer' reads as an exemplary reply; split it into two pieces and turn them round together.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesop was the ancient Greek author credited with the famous collection of animal fables.

clue.text: Identified coins banks provided with old penny

indicators.note: banks line both sides of a river, so one piece flanks the other

parts.note: specie is money in the form of coins
'provided' means on condition that, like if
d was the abbreviation for a penny in pre-decimal British money

explanation.surface: Someone recognised which coins banks handed over along with an old penny.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banks' looks like the institutions dealing in coins, but it is a verb: the coin word lines both sides of a condition word.
explanation.definitionFit: To specify something is to name or state it precisely, so specified means named or picked out.

clue.text: Lavish person boozing after opening of Pinot

indicators.note: the opening of anything is its start, so only the first letter is kept

parts.note: first letter of the wine name
a lush is a heavy drinker

explanation.surface: An extravagant drinker who gets going once the Pinot is opened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lavish' could describe the drinker in the surface, but it is the definition; 'after' places the drinker behind the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Plush means luxurious and expensively furnished, close in sense to lavish or opulent.

clue.text: Old city's ceremony — bet it is occasionally ignored

parts.note: pomp is ceremonial splendour

indicators.note: ignoring something only now and then means every other letter is dropped and the rest kept

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters, with the rest dropped

explanation.surface: An ancient city's rituals, where a wager is sometimes overlooked.
explanation.walkthrough: The kept letters come from the even positions of the three words run together.
explanation.definitionFit: Pompeii is the Roman town buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79, an ancient settlement.

clue.text: Love may be so fully embraced by a French revolutionary

indicators.note: something embraced is held in arms, so it sits inside the surrounding piece

parts.note: un is the French for a
a red is a communist revolutionary
quite can mean completely

explanation.surface: A French revolutionary's romance, fully embraced, perhaps returned in kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' after 2-down suggests reversal again, but here it is RED, wrapped round the word for fully.
explanation.definitionFit: Unrequited love is a passion not returned by its object, a familiar idiom of romantic poetry.

clue.text: Clue antelope crosses river in remote area

parts.note: a hint is a clue

indicators.note: to cross something is to straddle it, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: an eland is a large African antelope
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A tip-off about an antelope fording a river somewhere in the wilds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clue' sounds like a crossword-about-crosswords word, but it simply gives HINT.
explanation.definitionFit: A hinterland is the remote back country lying far behind a coast or major town.

clue.text: Fries cold joints

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
hips are joints of the body

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fries' looks like a verb about cooking joints of meat, but it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Chips is the British word for thin fried potato strips, which Americans call french fries.

clue.text: It's used when pressing matter is resolved, saving time working

indicators.note: to resolve can mean to break down into parts, so the letters are reformed
saving can mean except, so one letter is left out

parts.note: taken as written
T is the abbreviation for time, here removed
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: Something deployed once an urgent issue is settled, saving time at work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pressing matter' reads as an urgent issue; 'pressing' belongs to the definition (ironing) and 'matter is' is the raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: A steam iron is the household appliance that smooths clothes with heat and vapour while ironing them.

clue.text: Like comic actor's crack in sequel that's shot

parts.note: to chap is to crack, as skin does in the cold

indicators.note: something shot is ruined or broken, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A comedian's wisecrack in a film sequel that's being shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' and 'shot' both sound like film-set talk; one is the verb chap, the other jumbles the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlie Chaplin was the silent film comedian, and the -esque suffix means in the style of him.

clue.text: Oats for one head of hotel, wanting European supply

indicators.note: supply here is the adverb of supple, so the letters bend into a new order
wanting means lacking, so one letter goes missing

parts.note: taken as written
E is the abbreviation for European, here removed

explanation.surface: A hotel manager short of European supplies of oats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of hotel' wants to give H, but all three words are fodder, and 'supply' is not a noun but means flexibly.
explanation.definitionFit: Oats are a classic example of wholesome, natural fare sold as nourishing diet produce.

clue.text: Makes very dear papa paella, say, during parts of match

indicators.note: something happening during a period falls within it, so these pieces go inside

parts.note: an over is a set of six balls in cricket
Papa is P in the NATO phonetic alphabet
paella is an example of a rice dish

explanation.surface: Dad charges a fortune for paella at the cricket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very dear' sounds affectionate beside 'papa', but it means expensive.
explanation.definitionFit: To overprice goods is to charge too much for them, making them excessively expensive.

clue.text: Cover staff back after a lot of resentment

indicators.note: a lot of something is not all of it, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: envy loses its final letter

indicators.note: going back means travelling the opposite way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a staff is a long pole

explanation.surface: Covering for a colleague returning after a long grudge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' reads as employees covering a shift, but it is a stick.
explanation.definitionFit: To envelop is to wrap up or surround something completely, so it covers it.

clue.text: Standard places to eat last of Victoria sponges

indicators.note: eating takes something inside, so the outer pieces swallow a letter

parts.note: par is the normal or standard level
sites are places

indicators.note: the last of anything is its end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the name

explanation.surface: The usual spots to finish off the remaining Victoria sponge cakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Victoria sponges' is a famous British cake, a jam-filled sponge, which disguises 'sponges' as the definition of freeloaders.
explanation.definitionFit: A sponge is a scrounger living off others, and parasites likewise feed on a host.

clue.text: Letter from India, one put in language from the east

parts.note: India is I in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: in an across entry, coming from the east means reading right to left
putting one thing in another places it inside

parts.note: Latin is a language
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A letter arriving from India, written in an eastern language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter from India' looks like correspondence; 'Letter' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An initial is the first character of a name, so it is a single alphabetic character.

clue.text: Drink from well in East London

indicators.note: Cockney speech of the East End drops the breathy sound at the start of words

parts.note: hale means healthy, as in hale and hearty

explanation.surface: Drinking water drawn from a well in the East End.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well' looks like a water source, but it is the adjective; East End Cockneys famously drop their aitches.
explanation.definitionFit: Ale is a type of beer, and a drink in the sense of an alcoholic beverage.

clue.text: More corpulent setter breaks into food store

indicators.note: a burglar who breaks into a place ends up inside it

parts.note: a larder is a pantry
the setter refers to themself as I

explanation.surface: A fatter crossword setter raids the pantry.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter is I in crosswords; the self-mocking picture fits the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Lardy is informal for fat, so its comparative describes someone fatter or more portly.

clue.text: Somewhat antipathetic, in essence displaying this?

definitions.text: Somewhat antipathetic, in essence displaying this?

indicators.note: somewhat means only part of, so the answer is a stretch of the following letters

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and through the next two

explanation.surface: Someone a little hostile at heart shows this quality.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: someone mildly antipathetic shows coldness.
explanation.definitionFit: Iciness is a chilly, unfriendly manner, which is what an antipathetic person shows towards others.

clue.text: Duff intel going around over offence

parts.note: a dud is something duff or useless

indicators.note: going around something encircles it, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: gen is British slang for information
O is the cricket scoring abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: Bad intelligence doing the rounds causes upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duff intel' reads as one phrase about bad information but splits into two separate pieces; duff is British slang for worthless.
explanation.definitionFit: Dudgeon means indignant resentment, as in taking offence or being in high dudgeon.

clue.text: Green coloured clothes drawn deceptively

indicators.note: to clothe something is to wrap it up, so one piece wears the other

parts.note: dyed means coloured
eco- means environmentally green

explanation.surface: Garments dyed green, sketched in a misleading way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothes' looks like a noun for garments, but it is a verb; 'drawn' means lured, not sketched.
explanation.definitionFit: To decoy is to lure into a trap by trickery, so decoyed means enticed by a ruse.

clue.text: Conformist feeling that lady's sharp to hold back in sermon

parts.note: her refers to a woman

indicators.note: to hold something is to grip it inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: a sharp image is distinct

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A woman's pointed remark, held back during a sermon, against following the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back in sermon' wants to be a reversal; it takes only the end letter, which slips into the word for sharp.
explanation.definitionFit: The herd instinct is the urge to think and act like the crowd, an idiom drawn from animals moving together.

clue.text: Say foreign ally, when retreating, gets shot?

indicators.note: retreating means moving backwards, so the joined pieces run the other way

parts.note: e.g. means for example, like say
ami is French for friend

explanation.surface: An overseas ally is shot while withdrawing from battle.
explanation.walkthrough: The war picture makes 'shot' sound violent; it is a photograph.
explanation.definitionFit: A shot is a photograph, and an image is a picture taken by a camera.

clue.text: Form of address once for large figure

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the archaic singular form of you
second meaning: informal short form of a thousand

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned way of addressing a heavyweight dignitary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Large figure' suggests a big person, but it is a number, a thousand.
explanation.definitionFit: Thou was the old intimate pronoun, and a thou is slang for one thousand pounds or units.

clue.text: Old French bread accompanying power lunch?

parts.note: bread is slang for money, and a sou was an old French coin
P is the abbreviation for power

explanation.surface: Old French bread served alongside a business lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread' and 'lunch' paint a meal; bread is money and 'power lunch' splits apart, with the question mark marking soup as one example of lunch.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowl of soup is a common midday meal, given here as an example signalled by the question mark.

clue.text: Players love runs by Gunners around box

indicators.note: around means encircling, so the outer pieces enclose another

parts.note: love is nil in tennis, shaped like O
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
the Royal Artillery, whose soldiers are gunners
a chest is a box

explanation.surface: Footballers love making runs with Arsenal around the penalty box.
explanation.walkthrough: Gunners is the nickname of Arsenal football club, which with 'box' makes a football scene; in crosswords Gunners are the Royal Artillery.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchestra is a band of musicians, and players is a common word for performers on instruments.

clue.text: Swift brute, rolling over, loves animal feed

indicators.note: rolling over turns something end over end, so the pieces are read backwards

parts.note: love is O, so two of them
hay is fodder for livestock

explanation.surface: A fast beast rolls over, loving its fodder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swift' looks like an adjective meaning fast, but it is Jonathan Swift, whose Gulliver's Travels has brutish creatures called Yahoos.
explanation.definitionFit: Yahoos are the coarse humanlike beasts in Gulliver's Travels, so a yahoo is a boorish lout.

clue.text: Looks for water, concealing whiskey measures

indicators.note: something concealed is out of sight, so a letter disappears from view

parts.note: to dowse is to search for underground water with a rod
Whiskey is W in the NATO phonetic alphabet, here removed

explanation.surface: Someone hunts for water while hiding their whiskey measures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concealing' usually wraps one piece round another; here the hidden letter simply vanishes.
explanation.definitionFit: A dose is a measured quantity of medicine, and a measure is a set amount of drink or drug.

clue.text: Cadge soft drug, at first, for sleeping policeman

parts.note: speed is slang for amphetamine
to bum a cigarette is to cadge one
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning soft

explanation.surface: Scrounging a soft drug first, for an officer asleep on duty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At first' moves the drug to the front, ahead of the other two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleeping policeman is the British name for a raised hump across a road that slows traffic.
